H1.text: A shopkeeper adds kilograms to kilograms. A clock adds minutes to minutes.

H2.text: But nobody adds kilograms to minutes. Why not? That one rule can catch a wrong formula.

H3.text: Aarav's classmate writes: distance equals speed times time, plus acceleration times time.

H4.text: Is it even possible? Aarav wants to know before doing a single experiment.

P1.text: Quick reminder. Length is L. Time is T. Mass is M.

P3.text: Speed is L T to the minus one.

P4.text: Acceleration is L T to the minus two.

R1.text: Now the big rule. It is called the principle of homogeneity of dimensions.

T1.text: Here it is. In a correct equation, every term must have the same dimensions.

R3.text: You can only add, subtract or equate things of the same kind.

R4.text: Three metres plus two metres is five metres. But three metres plus two seconds is nothing at all.

S1.text: Let's test this on Aarav's bicycle. It starts at two metres per second and speeds up.

S2.text: Watch. Speed times time grows in metres. Half a t squared also grows in metres.

S3.text: Add them, and you get x, the distance gone, also in metres. The graph curves upward.

S4.text: Slow-mo replay. Velocity, in blue, keeps growing. Acceleration, in red, stays the same.

S5.text: Now his last term, a times t. It comes out in metres per second.

S6.text: Metres plus metres per second? That is like adding kilograms to minutes. It cannot be done.

D1.text: Let's check the correct formula properly, one step at a time.

D2.text: Step one. The left side, x, is a length. Its dimensions are L.

D3.text: Step two. u t is velocity times time. L T to the minus one, times T, gives L.

D4.text: Step three. The half is a pure number. L T to the minus two, times T squared, gives L.

D5.text: Step four. Every term is L. So the equation is dimensionally consistent.

B1.text: Now the classmate's formula. Its last term is acceleration times time.

B2.text: That is L T to the minus one. A speed, not a length. So the formula is surely wrong.

L1.text: But why must every term match? Follow the links.

L2.text: A true law must stay true in any unit. Let's run the bicycle for two seconds.

L3.text: In seconds, both formulas give six. His formula even looks right!

L4.text: Now measure the same time in minutes. The correct formula still gives six metres.

L5.text: But his last term jumps to one hundred and twenty. Now his formula says one hundred and twenty four.

L6.text: Same ride, two answers. A mixed formula changes with the unit, so it can never be a law of nature.

K1.text: Side by side. With a half, the formula passes. It gives six metres, just like the real ride.

K2.text: With a two, it still passes, since a number has no dimensions. But it says twelve metres. Wrong.

K3.text: Now you try. If a formula passes the dimension check, is it surely correct? Pause the video and decide.

K4.text: No! Fails means surely wrong. Passes means only possibly right. Numbers like a half slip through.

G1.text: One more rule. Whatever goes inside sine, cosine, log or e to the power must be a pure number.

G3.text: An angle is arc length divided by radius. Length over length. So an angle has no dimensions.

G4.text: Your turn. In y equals A sine omega t, t is time. What must the dimensions of omega be? Pause and decide.

G5.text: T to the minus one! Omega times t must be a pure number, so omega has to cancel the T.

W2.text: Check the formula v squared equals u squared plus two a s. Then use it.

W3.text: v squared and u squared both have dimensions L squared T to the minus two.

W4.text: Two a s is L T to the minus two, times L. Also L squared T to the minus two. It passes.

W5.text: Now a cycle starts at three metres per second, and speeds up at two metres per second squared, over four metres.

W6.text: v squared is nine plus sixteen, which is twenty five. So the final speed is five metres per second.

X2.text: Many students think every quantity in an equation must have the same dimensions.

X3.text: Not true. Only terms that are added or equated must match. In F equals m a, mass and acceleration differ, and that is fine.

E1.text: Where is this asked? As questions on the dimensions of constants, or on the formula that is wrong.

Q1.text: Exam level now. x equals alpha sine beta t, plus gamma t squared. What are the dimensions of alpha beta over gamma? Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is C. The dimensions of time.

A2.text: Alpha is a length. Beta t must be a pure number, so beta is T to the minus one.

A3.text: Gamma t squared is a length, so gamma is L T to the minus two. Divide, and only T is left.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Why can distance never be u t plus a t?

Y3.text: Two. If a formula passes the dimension check, is it surely correct?

Y4.text: Three. In y equals A sine omega t, what are the dimensions of omega?

N1.text: Next time: can this rule build a formula from nothing? Applications of dimensional analysis.
